textualConstraints.claim: After Succoth Israel camped at Etham at the edge of the wilderness.
The movement to Pi-hahiroth is described as turning back from the Etham stage rather than simply continuing in a straight line.
The camp is relationally described before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh's interpretation requires a route that appeared constrained by wilderness and water and vulnerable to chariot pursuit.
After the sea passage the itinerary enters the wilderness of Shur/Etham, linking the crossing to the eastern desert margin.
The Hebrew yam in the immediate narrative identifies the water crossed, while the wider designation yam suph does not by itself select one modern lake or the modern Gulf of Suez coastline.
Migdol can function as a place-name connected with a frontier tower or fort, but the term does not uniquely identify one excavated installation without independent evidence.
Baal-zephon supplies an orientation landmark or cultic place-name; multiple ancient sites associated with Baal-zephon prevent unique identification from the name alone.

candidates.label: Northern coastal / Sirbonic corridor
supports: Baal-zephon traditions are strongly represented in the north-eastern Delta and coastal sphere.
A coastal barrier-lagoon setting can produce water-and-wilderness constraint.
problems: The identification depends on disputed correlations of Baal-zephon and the sea terminology.
It lengthens or reorganizes the relation to the Wadi Tumilat/Etham sequence.
No secure inscription identifies the Exodus camp.

candidates.label: Ballah Lakes / north isthmus corridor
supports: It lies near the eastern Delta frontier and north-south military routes.
Former lake and marsh systems provide a plausible constrained approach.
The corridor can be related to a turn from the Wadi Tumilat/Etham axis.
problems: Ancient shorelines and lake connectivity changed through time and require palaeoenvironmental reconstruction.
No excavated site is securely named Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon together.
The proposed crossing point varies substantially among reconstructions.

candidates.label: Lake Timsah / Bitter Lakes corridor
supports: It preserves a close relation to the Wadi Tumilat and the eastern wilderness margin.
The lake basin can fit the narrative movement from settlement corridor to constrained waterside camp.
It has a long history in scholarly southern-isthmus route reconstructions.
problems: Modern canal and lake geography cannot be projected directly into the Late Bronze Age.
The location of Baal-zephon remains unproven.
Different reconstructions place Etham, Migdol and the crossing on incompatible points.
